title: Factorising
examples: When do I need to use the DOTS method?
What is the difference between factoring and expanding?
Can I factorise something that has more than three terms?

explain.say: Today we are learning how to factorise expressions.

items: Factorising means writing an expression as a product
It is the reverse of expanding brackets

explain.say: First, we look for a common factor across all terms.
Next, we factorise simple quadratics where the leading coefficient is one.
Then, we tackle quadratics where the leading coefficient is not one.
Finally, we use the DOTS method for harder factorising problems.
In real life, we factorise when calculating the area of complex shapes.

faq.q: What is the difference between factorising and expanding?
faq.a: Expanding means multiplying brackets together to get one expression. Factorising means doing the opposite, which is breaking an expression down into its factors.

faq.q: When should I use the DOTS method?
faq.a: You use DOTS when you see two perfect squares separated by a minus sign. The pattern is always a squared term minus another squared term.
asks: What is the pattern for DOTS?
Does DOTS only work with numbers?

faq.q: Do I always have to look for a common factor first?
faq.a: Yes, it is usually best practice to check for a greatest common factor first. This simplifies the remaining terms before you apply other methods.
asks: Should I always factor out the GCF?
What if there is no common factor?

faq.q: What if the quadratic has three terms but no common factor?
faq.a: If there is no common factor, you should check if it fits the pattern for a perfect square trinomial or the difference of two squares.

faq.q: Can I factorise an expression with many terms?
faq.a: You can, but you must look for a common factor shared by every single term first. Then you might look for grouping methods.
asks: What if I have four terms?
Does the number of terms matter?

facts: Factorising is the process of writing an algebraic expression as a product of its factors.
The greatest common factor (GCF) must be found before attempting other factorising methods.
The difference of two squares follows the pattern a² - b² = (a - b)(a + b).
When factorising a quadratic like x² + 5x + 6, you look for two numbers that multiply to six and add to five.
